sub.en: Look at each sentence. Which half takes will, and which half does not?

items.q: If you ___ too hard, people will think you are aggressive.
items.why: The if-clause takes the Present Simple, even though it is about the future. Only the other half takes will.

items.q: If you don’t shake hands, some people ___ offended.
If it rains, we ___ meet inside instead.
items.why: might replaces will when you are less sure — the if-clause does not change.

items.q: What ___ you do if he offers his hand?
You won’t make a good impression ___ you look at them.
items.why: unless = if … not. “Unless you look at them” means “if you don’t look at them”.

items.q: If nobody ___ hands any more, greetings will change completely.
___ you get it wrong, people will think you are unfriendly.
In some countries you ___ take your shoes off — it’s the custom.
items.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 23: have to for a rule that comes from outside.

acts.title: The rise and fall of the handshake
text: The handshake is about three thousand years old and the usual explanation for it is wrong. It is often said that people shook hands to show they held no weapon. Historians think it was simpler: it was how you sealed an agreement, and the hand was the part of the body you could see.

It has never been universal. In Japan a bow does the same job; in parts of the Middle East a handshake between men is soft and long, and a strong grip reads as aggression, not confidence; in Tibet, for a period, people greeted each other by putting out their tongue.

And it carries real risk. Studies have found that hands carry more germs than almost any other part of the body, and that a fist bump transfers a small fraction of what a handshake does. In 2020 many workplaces stopped shaking hands entirely, and some never went back.

So what happens next? If the handshake disappears, something will take its place, because greetings are not optional: if you refuse to greet somebody at all, they will read it as an insult, in every culture anybody has studied.

The likely answer is that we will keep several. A nod for colleagues, a hug for friends, a handshake for the moments that still feel formal. Unless you know which one the other person expects, you will get it wrong — and you will have about two seconds to decide.

The long one, as in “eat”: disease, meat, easy.
The short one, as in “bread”: health, instead, weather, already.

items.sit: You describe a greeting between two colleagues who meet every day.

lines.s: What do you do at a first meeting here? 🤝
___ it’s work, you shake hands. Otherwise a nod. 🙂
And if I get it wrong?
Nothing happens. People ___ think you’re foreign, that’s all. 👀
What about the picnic on Saturday?
If it ___, we might meet inside. 🌧
Then we ___ eat outside — nobody has decided. 🤷

write.q: Write six first-conditional sentences about greetings and habits in your country. Use will in three of them, might in two, and unless in one. Remember that the if-clause takes the present.
write.model: If you meet somebody for the first time here, you will usually shake hands. If you are a woman meeting a woman, you might not — it depends on the family. If you go into somebody’s home, you will have to take your shoes off, and if you forget, nobody will say anything but everybody will notice. If you refuse tea, people might think you are unhappy with them. Unless you know the family well, take something small with you. If you do all this, you will be fine.

speak.q: Answer out loud: What will happen if a visitor doesn’t shake hands here? What will you do if it rains at the weekend? What might change about greetings in ten years?
speak.model: If a visitor doesn’t shake hands, nobody will say anything, but people will notice. If it rains at the weekend, we might stay at home. In ten years I think we will keep several greetings — a nod at work and a hug for friends.
